name: Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries
title: Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries
answer: Autonomous entities and AI fiduciaries covers systems that act on someone's behalf with limited or no human sign off at the moment of action, from trading and procurement agents to software that manages money, data or care for a named beneficiary. The legal question is not whether the software is clever but whether a duty of loyalty and care can attach to a party that is not a person, and who answers when it fails. This sits inside the emerging legal frameworks tracked on this site, alongside the 150 active AI lawsuits and 29 AI case law precedents already catalogued.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on ordinary cloud infrastructure, usually a model or rules engine wrapped in an execution layer that can call payment rails, APIs, messaging and file stores without a human pressing send. Identity, permissions and audit logging are the load bearing parts, because a fiduciary claim depends on showing what the agent was authorised to do and what it actually did. Most deployments keep a human in the loop for high value or irreversible actions, and the design of that checkpoint is where much of the legal exposure sits.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by writing a mandate, encoding it as instructions and limits, then testing the agent against scenarios before it touches live accounts. Lawyers and compliance staff map each automated decision to the duty it is meant to serve, whether that is best interest, prudence, disclosure or avoidance of conflicts. Records are kept so that a later review can reconstruct the reasoning, and periodic human review is used to catch drift between the written mandate and the agent's behaviour.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on agency law, fiduciary duties, consumer protection and sector rules, and on who bears liability when an autonomous entity causes loss. Provenance matters because a court or regulator will ask who configured the agent, what data it was trained on, which version acted, and whether the beneficiary consented. The site's 229 compliance and regulation pages and 7166 state AI bills show how fragmented this is, with disclosure, record keeping and human oversight appearing as recurring themes rather than one settled standard.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect more attempts to register or licence AI fiduciaries, clearer rules on when an agent's act binds its principal, and insurance products written around automated mandates. Courts will keep testing whether existing doctrines stretch to non human actors or whether new categories are needed, and the 92 intellectual property suits already tracked suggest disputes will arrive through many doors at once. The practical direction is toward auditable agents with bounded authority, named human accountability and evidence that the duty was designed in rather than assumed.
